about: Circulation and Breathing (MBBS0015) is the third of the four systems modules in UCL's MBBS Year 1, running across Terms 1 and 2 (in 2026–27, from December to early February, between CIF Weeks A and B). UCL's module page says it introduces the cardiovascular and respiratory systems: how we breathe, how oxygen and nutrients reach the tissues, how waste is removed, and the drugs used to treat disorders of these systems. Its aims also cover responses to changing metabolic demand, the origins and risk factors of common diseases, basic clinical skills and tests, and an introduction to clinical decision-making. The module is taught in person and carries 0 credits; Year 1 knowledge is tested in the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests (online SBA and VSA papers).

notes.h: Respiratory structure and the mechanics of breathing
notes.body:
UCL's module page says Circulation and Breathing begins with how we breathe. You need the anatomy of the airways and the physics that moves air in and out.

Airways: conducting and respiratory zones
- Air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx and trachea. The trachea divides at the carina, at roughly the level of the sternal angle (about T4/T5).
- The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually enter the right side.
- The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower); the left has two (upper, with the lingula, and lower).
- Conducting zone: trachea to terminal bronchioles. It warms, humidifies and filters air but takes no part in gas exchange, so it forms the anatomical dead space (roughly 150 mL in an adult; approximate).
- Respiratory zone: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli, where gas exchange happens.

The alveolus
- Type I pneumocytes are thin, flat cells covering most of the alveolar surface, giving a very short diffusion distance.
- Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and can divide to replace type I cells.
- Alveolar macrophages clear particles and microbes.

Pleura and the pressures
- Each lung is covered by visceral pleura; the parietal pleura lines the chest wall. Between them is a thin fluid-filled pleural space.
- The lungs tend to recoil inwards and the chest wall outwards, so intrapleural pressure is normally below atmospheric (negative). If air enters the space (pneumothorax), that link is lost and the lung collapses.

Inspiration and expiration
- Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure × volume is constant. Increase thoracic volume and alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric, so air flows in.
- Quiet inspiration is active: the diaphragm (supplied by the phrenic nerve, C3–C5) contracts and flattens, and the external intercostals raise the ribs.
- Quiet expiration is passive: the muscles relax and elastic recoil of the lungs returns them to resting volume.
- Forced breathing recruits accessory muscles: sternocleidomastoid and scalenes for inspiration; internal intercostals and abdominal muscles for forced expiration.

Compliance and surfactant
- Compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure (ΔV/ΔP). Fibrosis lowers compliance (stiff lungs); emphysema raises it (floppy lungs that recoil poorly).
- Surface tension in the alveolar fluid lining tends to collapse alveoli. The law of Laplace (P = 2T/r) says smaller alveoli would need higher pressure to stay open. Surfactant lowers surface tension, more so in smaller alveoli, stabilising them and reducing the work of breathing. Preterm babies can lack surfactant (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome).

Lung volumes (typical young adult values, all approximate)
- Tidal volume about 500 mL; total lung capacity about 6 L; residual volume about 1.2 L; vital capacity roughly 4.5–5 L.
- Functional residual capacity (FRC, volume left after a quiet breath out) is about 2.4 L. It is the point where inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall recoil.
- Residual volume and FRC cannot be measured by simple spirometry because spirometry only measures air that moves.

Ventilation
- Minute ventilation = tidal volume × respiratory rate (e.g. 0.5 L × 12 = 6 L/min).
- Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate (e.g. 0.35 L × 12 = 4.2 L/min). Rapid shallow breathing wastes a larger share of each breath on dead space.

Exam tips: be able to explain why quiet expiration is passive, calculate alveolar ventilation, and link compliance changes to fibrosis and emphysema.

notes.h: Gas exchange, gas transport and the control of breathing
notes.body:
The module's aim is to explain how oxygen reaches the tissues and how waste such as carbon dioxide is removed. That depends on diffusion across the alveolar wall, carriage in blood and control of ventilation.

Diffusion (Fick's law)
- Rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area × diffusion constant × partial-pressure difference ÷ membrane thickness.
- So gas exchange falls if area falls (emphysema), thickness rises (fibrosis, pulmonary oedema) or the pressure gradient falls (high altitude).
- CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, so it diffuses much more readily; diffusion problems show up first as low oxygen.

Partial pressures (approximate, at sea level)
- Inspired PO₂ after humidification is about 0.21 × (101.3 − 6.3) ≈ 20 kPa.
- Alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = PIO₂ − PaCO₂/R, with respiratory quotient R about 0.8. So PAO₂ ≈ 20 − 5.3/0.8 = 20 − 6.6 ≈ 13.4 kPa (about 100 mmHg).
- Arterial PO₂ is normally a little lower than alveolar; arterial PCO₂ is about 5.3 kPa (40 mmHg). Mixed venous PO₂ is about 5.3 kPa.
- 1 kPa ≈ 7.5 mmHg.

Oxygen transport
- About 98% of oxygen in arterial blood is bound to haemoglobin; very little is dissolved.
- Each gram of haemoglobin can carry about 1.34 mL O₂. With Hb 150 g/L and saturation of about 98%, arterial content is about 1.34 × 150 × 0.98 ≈ 197 mL/L, plus roughly 3 mL/L dissolved, so about 200 mL/L.
- Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × arterial O₂ content, e.g. 5 L/min × 200 mL/L ≈ 1,000 mL/min, far more than resting consumption (roughly 250 mL/min).

The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve
- Sigmoid because of cooperative binding: once one haem binds O₂, the others bind more easily.
- The flat upper part protects saturation when alveolar PO₂ falls a little; the steep middle part lets tissues unload a lot of O₂ for a small fall in PO₂.
- Right shift (lower affinity, more unloading): raised CO₂, raised H⁺ (lower pH; the Bohr effect), raised temperature, raised 2,3-BPG. These are exactly the conditions in active muscle.
- Left shift (higher affinity): the opposite changes, fetal haemoglobin and carbon monoxide. CO also binds haemoglobin far more avidly than O₂, reducing carrying capacity.

Carbon dioxide transport (approximate shares)
- About 70% as bicarbonate: in red cells carbonic anhydrase speeds CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; bicarbonate leaves the cell in exchange for chloride (the chloride shift).
- About 20–25% as carbamino compounds, mainly bound to haemoglobin.
- About 5–10% dissolved.
- Haldane effect: deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂, helping uptake in tissues and release in lungs.

Ventilation–perfusion matching
- Ideal exchange needs ventilation (V) matched to blood flow (Q). Low V/Q (e.g. a blocked airway) acts like a shunt and causes hypoxaemia; high V/Q (e.g. a pulmonary embolus) behaves like dead space.
- Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli.

Control of breathing
- Rhythm is generated by groups of neurones in the medulla, modified by the pons.
- Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H⁺ in cerebrospinal fluid, which reflects arterial PCO₂. This is the main minute-to-minute drive.
- Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic bodies (vagus) respond to low PaO₂ (strongly once it falls to roughly 8 kPa or below), raised PaCO₂ and raised H⁺.

Exam tips: practise the alveolar gas equation, list the factors that shift the dissociation curve, and explain why CO₂ is the main drive to breathe.

notes.h: Structure of the heart, the cardiac cycle and its electrical activity
notes.body:
The heart is two pumps in series: the right side sends blood to the lungs and the left side to the rest of the body.

Chambers, valves and vessels
- Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the superior and inferior venae cavae, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and leaves through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
- Oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve.
- The left ventricle wall is much thicker because it generates far higher pressure. Typical peak systolic pressures (approximate): left ventricle about 120 mmHg, right ventricle about 25 mmHg.
- Coronary arteries arise just above the aortic valve. The left main stem divides into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries; the right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove. The left ventricle is perfused mainly in diastole, because contraction compresses its intramural vessels.

The cardiac cycle
- Atrial systole tops up ventricular filling at the end of diastole.
- Isovolumetric contraction: ventricles contract, pressure rises, the atrioventricular valves close (first heart sound, S1) and all valves are shut.
- Ejection: ventricular pressure exceeds aortic and pulmonary pressure, the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected.
- Isovolumetric relaxation: pressure falls, the aortic and pulmonary valves close (second heart sound, S2).
- Filling: when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure the atrioventricular valves open and the ventricles fill, mostly passively.
- Valve opening is normally silent. S2 splits physiologically on inspiration because more venous return to the right side delays pulmonary valve closure.

Electrical conduction
- The sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium near the superior vena cava is the normal pacemaker.
- The impulse spreads through the atria to the atrioventricular (AV) node, which delays conduction (roughly 0.1 s, approximate) so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
- It then passes down the bundle of His, left and right bundle branches and Purkinje fibres, so the ventricles contract from apex upwards.

Action potentials
- Ventricular myocytes: phase 0 rapid depolarisation by fast Na⁺ influx; phase 1 brief repolarisation (transient K⁺ outflow); phase 2 plateau as L-type Ca²⁺ influx balances K⁺ efflux; phase 3 repolarisation by K⁺ efflux; phase 4 stable resting potential. The long plateau gives a long refractory period, preventing tetanic contraction.
- Pacemaker cells have no stable resting potential. A slow depolarisation (the 'funny' current, mainly Na⁺ through HCN channels, then T-type Ca²⁺) reaches threshold and L-type Ca²⁺ channels produce the upstroke.
- Sympathetic stimulation (noradrenaline on β1 receptors) steepens the pacemaker slope and raises heart rate and contractility. Vagal stimulation (acetylcholine on M2 receptors) slows the rate.

Excitation–contraction coupling
- Ca²⁺ entering during the plateau triggers more Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release). Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, allowing actin–myosin cross-bridges to form.

The ECG
- P wave: atrial depolarisation. PR interval: conduction through the atria and AV node (normally about 0.12–0.20 s). QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation (normally under about 0.12 s). T wave: ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS.

Exam tips: be able to sequence the cardiac cycle with pressures, valve events and heart sounds, and match each ion current to its action-potential phase.

notes.h: Cardiac output, blood pressure and responses to changing demand
notes.body:
UCL's module aims include how these systems respond to the body's changing metabolic needs. The key relationships below let you explain posture, exercise and blood loss.

Cardiac output
- Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate (HR) × stroke volume (SV). Typical resting values are about 70 beats/min × 70 mL ≈ 5 L/min (approximate).
- Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume (EDV) − end-systolic volume (ESV), e.g. 120 − 50 = 70 mL.
- Ejection fraction = SV ÷ EDV, e.g. 70 ÷ 120 ≈ 58%. A normal ejection fraction is above roughly 50–55%.

What sets stroke volume
- Preload: how much the ventricle is stretched at the end of diastole, mainly set by venous return. The Frank–Starling mechanism means a greater stretch gives a stronger contraction, so output matches input.
- Afterload: the load the ventricle works against during ejection, largely arterial pressure. A higher afterload reduces stroke volume.
- Contractility: the strength of contraction at any given preload; raised by sympathetic stimulation via β1 receptors.

Blood pressure and resistance
- Mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≈ CO × total peripheral resistance (TPR); strictly, the driving pressure is MAP minus central venous pressure.
- At rest, MAP ≈ diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure, because the heart spends longer in diastole. For 120/80 mmHg: 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
- Poiseuille's relationship: resistance is proportional to viscosity × length ÷ radius⁴. Halving a vessel's radius raises resistance 16-fold. Arterioles are the main resistance vessels and adjust flow to each organ.
- Veins are capacitance vessels and hold most of the blood volume (roughly two-thirds; approximate).

Capillary exchange (Starling forces)
- Filtration out of capillaries is driven by capillary hydrostatic pressure; plasma proteins (mainly albumin) exert an oncotic pressure that holds fluid in.
- Normally a little more fluid leaves than returns; the excess goes back via lymphatics.
- Oedema follows raised hydrostatic pressure (heart failure), low plasma proteins (e.g. nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), leaky capillaries (inflammation) or blocked lymphatics.

Short-term control: the baroreceptor reflex
- Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus) signal to the medulla.
- On standing, blood pools in the leg veins, venous return and stroke volume fall, and arterial pressure dips. Baroreceptor firing falls, so sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls: heart rate, contractility, arteriolar constriction and venoconstriction all increase, restoring pressure within seconds.
- Failure of this response causes postural (orthostatic) hypotension.

Longer-term control
- The kidney controls blood volume. Low renal perfusion releases renin, which leads to angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, thirst) and sodium and water retention.

Responses to exercise
- Cardiac output can rise several-fold (roughly four to five times resting in a fit young adult; approximate) through higher heart rate and stroke volume.
- Local metabolites (raised CO₂, H⁺, K⁺ and adenosine, low O₂) dilate muscle arterioles, so TPR falls; sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from gut and skin.
- Systolic pressure rises; diastolic pressure changes little or falls slightly.
- Ventilation rises with oxygen demand, and the dissociation curve shifts right in muscle, increasing oxygen extraction.

Exam tips: always write the equations (CO = HR × SV; MAP ≈ CO × TPR) and use them to reason step by step through a scenario.

notes.h: Origins and risk factors of common cardiovascular diseases
notes.body:
UCL lists the origins and risk factors of common cardiovascular diseases as an aim. Most of this teaching revolves around atherosclerosis, hypertension and heart failure.

Atherosclerosis: how plaques form
- Endothelial dysfunction is the starting point (from hypertension, smoking, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes and disturbed blood flow at branch points).
- LDL enters the vessel wall and becomes oxidised. Monocytes are attracted, enter the intima and become macrophages, which take up oxidised LDL and become lipid-laden foam cells. These form the fatty streak, the earliest visible lesion.
- Smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and lay down collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich, necrotic core: the mature plaque.
- Stable plaques with thick caps narrow the lumen gradually and cause symptoms on exertion (e.g. stable angina, intermittent claudication).
- Unstable plaques have thin caps, large lipid cores and many inflammatory cells. Rupture or erosion exposes the core, platelets adhere and aggregate, and a thrombus forms, causing acute coronary syndrome or ischaemic stroke.

Risk factors
- Non-modifiable: increasing age, male sex, family history of premature cardiovascular disease, and ethnicity (for example, higher risk in people of South Asian family origin).
- Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised non-HDL (including LDL) cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet and excess alcohol. Chronic kidney disease and some inflammatory conditions also raise risk.
- Risk factors multiply rather than simply add. In UK primary care, QRISK3 estimates a person's 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke to guide prevention.

Ischaemic heart disease
- Angina is chest pain from myocardial ischaemia, when oxygen supply cannot meet demand.
- Acute coronary syndrome includes unstable angina and myocardial infarction; most cases follow plaque rupture with thrombosis.

Hypertension
- Most adult hypertension is primary (essential), with no single identifiable cause; a minority is secondary (e.g. renal disease, primary hyperaldosteronism).
- In England, NICE guideline NG136 diagnoses hypertension when clinic BP is 140/90 mmHg or more and ambulatory (daytime) or home monitoring averages 135/85 mmHg or more. Stage 1 is clinic 140/90 to 159/99 with an ambulatory or home average of 135/85 to 149/94; stage 2 is clinic 160/100 or more (below 180/120) with an average of 150/95 or more; severe hypertension is clinic systolic 180 or more or diastolic 120 or more.
- Hypertension damages arteries and is a major risk factor for stroke, coronary disease, heart failure and kidney disease.

Heart failure
- A clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs at normal filling pressures.
- Common causes: ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, valve disease and cardiomyopathy.
- Classified by ejection fraction. The European Society of Cardiology (2021) uses reduced (40% or less), mildly reduced (41–49%) and preserved (50% or more). Check current UK guidance, as cut-offs differ slightly between guidelines.
- Neurohormonal activation (sympathetic system, renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system) initially supports output but worsens failure in the long run; this is why several heart-failure drugs block these systems.

Other conditions you may meet
- Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular rhythm; stagnant blood in the atria can form clots that cause stroke.
- Venous thromboembolism: Virchow's triad of stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel-wall injury explains the risk factors (immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen-containing medicines).

Exam tips: be able to draw the stages of plaque development and explain why plaque rupture, not just narrowing, causes heart attacks.

notes.h: Origins and risk factors of common respiratory diseases
notes.body:
Respiratory disease is often grouped by what it does to airflow and lung volumes. The two big patterns are obstructive and restrictive.

Obstructive vs restrictive
- Obstructive disease narrows the airways so air cannot be blown out quickly: FEV₁ falls more than FVC and the FEV₁/FVC ratio is low (below 0.7 is the usual UK threshold for COPD in NICE guidance). Examples: asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis.
- Restrictive disease limits lung expansion: FVC is reduced and the ratio is normal or high. Examples: pulmonary fibrosis, chest-wall deformity, obesity, neuromuscular weakness.

Asthma
- Chronic airway inflammation with variable airflow obstruction and airway hyper-responsiveness. Symptoms (wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough) vary over time and are often worse at night or early morning.
- Many cases are type 2 ('eosinophilic') inflammation: Th2 cytokines, IgE-mediated mast-cell activation, eosinophils, mucus hypersecretion and smooth-muscle contraction. Over time airway remodelling can occur.
- Risk factors and triggers: atopy (eczema, hay fever), family history, allergens, viral infections, cold air, exercise, smoke and occupational exposures. Some drugs (e.g. non-selective beta-blockers) can trigger bronchospasm.
- The joint BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline (2024) emphasises objective tests to confirm the diagnosis, such as FeNO or blood eosinophils, then spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, and peak-flow variability where spirometry is not available.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
- Persistent, progressive airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, with chronic bronchitis and emphysema in varying mixes.
- Chronic bronchitis: mucous gland hyperplasia and productive cough.
- Emphysema: permanent enlargement of airspaces with destruction of alveolar walls. Loss of elastic recoil lets small airways collapse on expiration, trapping air.
- Smoking is the main cause in the UK. Smoking typically causes centriacinar emphysema, worst in the upper lobes. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema, worst in the lower lobes, often in younger people.
- Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked. For example, 20 a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years.
- Other causes: occupational dusts, and biomass smoke in many countries.

Lung cancer
- Smoking is the dominant risk factor; others include radon, asbestos and air pollution.
- Main types: non-small-cell (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma) and small-cell carcinoma.

Infection
- Community-acquired pneumonia is most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Risk factors include older age, smoking, chronic lung disease and immunosuppression.
- CURB-65 helps judge severity: Confusion, Urea above 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate 30/min or more, low Blood pressure (systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 mmHg or less), age 65 or over.
- Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spreads by airborne droplets.

Pulmonary embolism
- Usually a clot from a deep vein of the leg. Virchow's triad explains the risk factors. A PE creates ventilated but unperfused lung (high V/Q).

Links between the systems
- Lung disease can strain the heart: chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale). Left heart failure can cause pulmonary oedema and breathlessness.

Exam tips: be ready to read a spirometry result, to name the emphysema patterns for smoking and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and to calculate pack-years.

notes.h: Basic clinical skills and tests of cardiorespiratory function
notes.body:
UCL's module aims include practising basic clinical skills and investigations to test cardiovascular and respiratory function. Year 1 teaching focuses on careful measurement and understanding what the numbers mean. Follow the techniques you are taught in clinical skills sessions; this note explains the principles.

Pulse
- Usually felt at the radial artery. Assess rate, rhythm (regular, regularly irregular, irregularly irregular), and in larger arteries (carotid, brachial) the character and volume.
- Count for a full 60 seconds if the rhythm is irregular.
- Adult resting heart rate is usually about 60–100 beats/min, though fit people often have lower rates.

Blood pressure
- Measured with an automated device or manually with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope over the brachial artery.
- Manual method: inflate the cuff above systolic pressure, deflate slowly; the first Korotkoff sound (phase I) marks systolic pressure and disappearance of the sounds (phase V) marks diastolic.
- Sources of error: wrong cuff size (too small overestimates, too large underestimates), arm not supported at heart level, talking, recent exercise, caffeine or smoking, and 'white-coat' effect.
- Postural (lying and standing) readings test the baroreceptor reflex.

Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
- Count breaths for a full minute, ideally without the patient noticing. A normal adult rate is about 12–20 breaths/min.
- Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxygen saturation (SpO₂) from the different absorption of red and infrared light by oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin. It can be inaccurate with poor perfusion, movement, nail varnish and carbon monoxide poisoning (carboxyhaemoglobin reads as oxygenated). Evidence has shown it can overestimate saturation in people with darker skin, which is an active area of work.
- British Thoracic Society guidance targets 94–98% SpO₂ for most acutely ill patients, and 88–92% for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some patients with COPD.

Examination
- Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations follow inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, after introducing yourself, gaining consent and washing hands.
- Auscultate the heart at the four classic valve areas and listen for S1 and S2. Over the lungs, compare both sides for breath sounds and added sounds (wheeze, crackles).

Peak expiratory flow and spirometry
- Peak expiratory flow (PEF) is the fastest flow in a forced breath out. It is cheap and useful for monitoring asthma; serial readings show variability. Compare with predicted values (based on age, sex and height) and the person's best.
- Spirometry measures FEV₁ (volume in the first second of forced expiration) and FVC (total volume forcibly exhaled). The FEV₁/FVC ratio separates obstructive from restrictive patterns. Bronchodilator reversibility testing compares readings before and after a bronchodilator.

The 12-lead ECG
- Standard paper speed is 25 mm/s: one small square (1 mm) = 0.04 s and one large square (5 mm) = 0.2 s.
- For a regular rhythm, heart rate ≈ 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves, or 1,500 ÷ number of small squares. Four large squares = 75 beats/min.
- For an irregular rhythm, count QRS complexes on a 10-second rhythm strip and multiply by 6.

Exam tips: know what can make each measurement wrong, and practise ECG rate calculations until they are automatic.

notes.h: Principles of drug treatment for heart and lung disease
notes.body:
UCL's module introduces how drugs are used to treat cardiovascular and respiratory disease. At Year 1 the focus is on mechanism: which target a drug acts on and what physiological change follows. This note gives no doses; always use the BNF and current guidance in practice.

Drugs acting on the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
- ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, causing vasodilation and less aldosterone (so less sodium and water retention). ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so bradykinin builds up, causing the typical dry cough and, rarely, angioedema. Other important effects: hyperkalaemia and changes in kidney function. Avoided in pregnancy.
- Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs, e.g. losartan) block the AT1 receptor, with similar benefits but little cough.

Beta-blockers
- Block β1 receptors in the heart, lowering heart rate and contractility (so less myocardial oxygen demand) and reducing renin release.
- Used in angina, after myocardial infarction, in some heart failure and to control rate in atrial fibrillation.
- Non-selective beta-blockers also block β2 receptors in the airways and can cause bronchospasm, so they are avoided in asthma.

Calcium-channel blockers
- Dihydropyridines (e.g. amlodipine) mainly dilate arterioles, lowering BP; ankle swelling is common.
- Rate-limiting types (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the heart and AV conduction.

Diuretics
- Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (e.g. indapamide) block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ co-transporter in the distal convoluted tubule.
- Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) block the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and are powerful; they relieve fluid overload in heart failure.
- Both can cause low potassium.

Hypertension: the NICE approach in England
- NICE NG136 starts most people aged under 55 who are not of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin on an ACE inhibitor or ARB; people aged 55 or over, and people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, usually start with a calcium-channel blocker. People with type 2 diabetes start with an ACE inhibitor or ARB whatever their age (an ARB is preferred over an ACE inhibitor for people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin). Lifestyle change comes first and throughout.

Lipids, platelets and clotting
- Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis; liver cells increase LDL receptors and LDL falls. Muscle aches are a known side effect.
- Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1) in platelets, reducing thromboxane A₂ for the platelet's lifetime.
- P2Y12 inhibitors (e.g. clopidogrel) block ADP-induced platelet activation.
- Anticoagulants act on the clotting cascade: warfarin antagonises vitamin K; direct oral anticoagulants inhibit factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran). Used in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism.
- Nitrates (e.g. glyceryl trinitrate) release nitric oxide, mainly dilating veins and lowering preload, which relieves angina.

Respiratory drugs
- Short-acting β2 agonists (e.g. salbutamol) stimulate β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, raising cAMP and causing relaxation. Effects: tremor, fast heart rate, low potassium. Long-acting β2 agonists (e.g. formoterol, salmeterol) last longer.
- Muscarinic antagonists (short-acting ipratropium; long-acting tiotropium) block M3 receptors, preventing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction.
- Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation by changing gene transcription; they treat the underlying inflammation in asthma.
- Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) block cysteinyl leukotriene receptors.
- In asthma, the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline moves away from using a short-acting β2 agonist alone, favouring treatments that always include an inhaled corticosteroid. Check the current guideline for treatment steps.

Exam tips: for each class, learn target, effect and one key adverse effect explained by the mechanism (e.g. ACE inhibitor cough from bradykinin).

The module's final aim is to begin developing clinical decision-making skills. In Year 1 this means learning a structured way of thinking, not memorising management plans.

From history to differential diagnosis
- Most diagnoses are suggested by the history. Use a structure: presenting complaint, history of the presenting complaint, past medical history, drug history and allergies, family history, social history (including smoking and pack-years, alcohol, occupation) and systems review.
- For pain, the SOCRATES framework is widely taught: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Time course, Exacerbating and relieving factors, Severity.
- A differential diagnosis is a list of possible causes, ordered by likelihood and by how dangerous it would be to miss them.

Chest pain and breathlessness as examples
- Chest pain: possible cardiac (acute coronary syndrome, stable angina, pericarditis), respiratory (pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia), aortic (dissection), gastrointestinal (reflux) and musculoskeletal causes.
- Breathlessness: cardiac (heart failure, arrhythmia), respiratory (asthma, COPD, pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, fibrosis), and others (anaemia, anxiety, metabolic acidosis).
- Link symptoms to physiology: for example, breathlessness lying flat (orthopnoea) suggests raised pulmonary venous pressure in left heart failure.

Tests and probability
- A test changes how likely a diagnosis is. How much it helps depends on how likely the diagnosis was before the test (pre-test probability).
- Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all people with the disease. A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps rule a disease out.
- Specificity = true negatives ÷ all people without the disease. A highly specific test, when positive, helps rule a disease in.
- Positive predictive value (PPV) = true positives ÷ all positive results. It depends on prevalence.

Worked example
- Test: sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%. Population of 1,000 with prevalence 10%: 100 have the disease, 900 do not.
- True positives = 90; false negatives = 10. True negatives = 0.8 × 900 = 720; false positives = 180.
- PPV = 90 ÷ (90 + 180) = 33%. NPV = 720 ÷ (720 + 10) ≈ 98.6%.
- So with low prevalence even a fairly good test produces many false positives, which is why tests should be targeted at people with a reasonable pre-test probability.

Recognising the unwell patient
- The ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) is used to assess and treat problems in order of threat to life.
- The National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2, Royal College of Physicians, 2017) scores respiration rate, oxygen saturation, whether the patient is on air or oxygen, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, level of consciousness or new confusion, and temperature. Higher totals trigger more urgent review.

Thinking errors (cognitive biases)
- Anchoring: sticking with the first diagnosis despite new information.
- Premature closure: stopping thinking once a plausible diagnosis is found.
- Availability bias: favouring diagnoses that come to mind easily, such as a recent memorable case.
- Safeguards include actively asking 'what else could this be?', checking for dangerous diagnoses and seeking senior input.

Shared decisions
- Decisions should be made with the patient. The GMC's guidance on decision making and consent (2020) expects doctors to discuss options, risks and benefits so the patient can choose.

Exam tips: practise building a 2 × 2 table from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence, and always justify a differential with features from the history.

questions.q: A person breathes with a tidal volume of 500 mL at 12 breaths per minute. Anatomical dead space is 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation is (500 − 150) mL × 12 = 4,200 mL/min, i.e. 4.2 L/min. 6.0 L/min is the minute ventilation (500 × 12), which forgets to remove dead space. 1.8 L/min is the dead-space ventilation (150 × 12), the part that does not reach the alveoli. 7.8 L/min comes from adding dead space to tidal volume (650 × 12) instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: Which cells in the alveolar wall secrete surfactant?
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant. Type I pneumocytes are the thin cells forming most of the gas-exchange surface, so they are the cells most often confused with type II. Goblet cells secrete mucus in the conducting airways, not surfactant. Alveolar macrophages are defensive cells that clear particles and microbes.

questions.q: Explain how air is drawn into the lungs during quiet inspiration and why quiet expiration is normally passive.
markScheme: Diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) contracts and flattens; external intercostals raise the ribs, increasing thoracic volume
Pleural coupling means lung volume increases with the chest wall; intrapleural pressure becomes more negative
Boyle's law: rising alveolar volume lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in down the pressure gradient
In quiet expiration the muscles relax and elastic recoil of the lungs (and surface tension) returns them to FRC
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric so air flows out without active muscle contraction
questions.modelAnswer: During quiet inspiration the diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), contracts and moves down, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs. Thoracic volume increases. Because the visceral and parietal pleura are held together by the thin pleural fluid layer, the lungs expand with the chest wall and intrapleural pressure becomes more negative. By Boyle's law, the rise in alveolar volume lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in until the pressures equalise. In quiet expiration the inspiratory muscles simply relax. The elastic tissue of the lungs and the surface tension of the alveolar lining make the lungs recoil, alveolar volume falls, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric and air flows out. No muscle contraction is needed, so quiet expiration is passive; forced expiration adds the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

questions.q: Which change increases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left?
questions.why: Cooling raises haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so a fall in temperature shifts the curve left. A rise in PCO₂ and a fall in pH both shift it right through the Bohr effect, which is why active muscle unloads more oxygen. More 2,3-BPG also shifts the curve right: it binds deoxyhaemoglobin and stabilises it, so it lowers affinity even though it might sound as if 'more binding' means more oxygen held.

questions.q: Inspired PO₂ (after humidification) is 20 kPa, arterial PCO₂ is 5.3 kPa and the respiratory quotient is 0.8. Using the alveolar gas equation, what is the alveolar PO₂?
questions.why: PAO₂ = PIO₂ − PaCO₂/R = 20 − 5.3/0.8 = 20 − 6.6 ≈ 13.4 kPa. About 14.7 kPa comes from subtracting PaCO₂ without dividing by R (20 − 5.3). About 6.6 kPa is just the CO₂ term (5.3/0.8), forgetting to subtract it from PIO₂. About 26.6 kPa comes from adding the CO₂ term instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: Describe how carbon dioxide is carried in the blood, giving approximate proportions, and explain the chloride shift.
markScheme: About 70% as bicarbonate (accept 60–70%)
Carbonic anhydrase in red cells catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; H⁺ buffered by haemoglobin
Chloride shift: HCO₃⁻ leaves red cell in exchange for Cl⁻ via an anion exchanger, maintaining electrical neutrality
About 20–25% as carbamino compounds (mostly with haemoglobin)
About 5–10% dissolved in plasma; Haldane effect increases carriage by deoxygenated blood
questions.modelAnswer: Most carbon dioxide, roughly 70%, is carried as bicarbonate. CO₂ diffuses into red cells, where carbonic anhydrase speeds its reaction with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. The H⁺ is buffered by haemoglobin. Bicarbonate moves out of the red cell into plasma in exchange for chloride through an anion-exchange protein; this is the chloride (Hamburger) shift, which keeps the cell electrically neutral. Around 20–25% of CO₂ binds to amino groups on proteins, mainly haemoglobin, as carbamino compounds, and about 5–10% is dissolved. These figures are approximate. Deoxygenated haemoglobin binds more CO₂ and H⁺ (the Haldane effect), so venous blood carries more CO₂ and releases it in the lungs when haemoglobin is oxygenated.

questions.q: Which ionic current mainly maintains the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular myocyte action potential?
questions.why: The plateau is held by inward Ca²⁺ through L-type channels, balanced against K⁺ efflux. The fast inward Na⁺ current causes the rapid upstroke in phase 0, not the plateau. The outward delayed-rectifier K⁺ current dominates phase 3, when the cell repolarises. The funny current drives the slow phase 4 depolarisation of pacemaker cells and is not what sustains the ventricular plateau.

questions.q: Which event produces the first heart sound?
options: Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
questions.why: The first heart sound is produced as the mitral and tricuspid valves close at the start of ventricular systole. Opening of the atrioventricular valves is normally silent; students sometimes assume any valve movement makes a sound. Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves produces the second heart sound. Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole is associated with a third heart sound, which is not the first sound.

questions.q: Describe the normal sequence of electrical conduction through the heart and explain the importance of the delay at the atrioventricular node.
markScheme: Impulse starts at the SA node in the right atrium (normal pacemaker)
Spreads across both atria causing atrial depolarisation/contraction
Delayed at the AV node, then passes down the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres to the ventricles
AV delay allows the atria to finish emptying into the ventricles before ventricular contraction (and limits the ventricular rate)
questions.modelAnswer: Each beat normally starts at the sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava. The impulse spreads across both atria, which depolarise and contract. It then reaches the atrioventricular node, where conduction slows. From there it travels down the bundle of His, the left and right bundle branches and the Purkinje fibres, so the ventricles depolarise rapidly, starting from the septum and apex. The delay at the AV node means the atria complete their contraction and top up ventricular filling before the ventricles contract. It also limits how many impulses reach the ventricles if the atrial rate becomes very fast.

questions.q: A patient's blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg at rest. What is the best estimate of mean arterial pressure?
questions.why: MAP ≈ diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure = 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg, because the heart spends about twice as long in diastole as systole at rest. 100 mmHg is the simple average of systolic and diastolic, which ignores the longer diastole. 40 mmHg is the pulse pressure, not a mean pressure. About 107 mmHg comes from subtracting one-third of pulse pressure from systolic, which wrongly weights the mean towards systole.

questions.q: If the radius of an arteriole halves while length and blood viscosity stay the same, how does its resistance to flow change?
questions.why: By Poiseuille's relationship resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴, so halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16. 'It doubles' assumes resistance is inversely proportional to radius in a simple linear way. 'It rises 4-fold' uses r², as if only cross-sectional area mattered. 'It falls to one-sixteenth' uses the right power but the wrong direction: a narrower vessel has more resistance, not less.

questions.q: Explain how the baroreceptor reflex maintains blood pressure when a person stands up quickly.
markScheme: Standing causes venous pooling in the legs, reducing venous return, preload and stroke volume, so arterial pressure falls
Reduced stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors lowers their firing (via CN IX and CN X) to the medulla
Increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic (vagal) outflow
Heart rate and contractility rise (β1); arteriolar constriction raises TPR; venoconstriction increases venous return
Pressure is restored within seconds (MAP ≈ CO × TPR); failure gives postural hypotension
questions.modelAnswer: On standing, gravity pools blood in the veins of the legs. Venous return and preload fall, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall and arterial pressure drops. The baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch are stretched less and fire less, sending fewer impulses along the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the cardiovascular centres in the medulla. The medulla responds by increasing sympathetic outflow and reducing vagal outflow. Heart rate and contractility rise through β1 receptors, arterioles constrict so total peripheral resistance rises, and veins constrict, pushing blood back towards the heart. Because mean arterial pressure is approximately cardiac output × total peripheral resistance, these changes restore pressure within seconds. If the reflex fails, for example in autonomic dysfunction, the person develops postural hypotension and may feel faint.

questions.q: In early atherosclerosis, which cells take up oxidised LDL in the intima to become foam cells and form the fatty streak?
questions.why: Monocytes enter the intima, become macrophages and take up oxidised LDL, becoming foam cells. Neutrophils are the classic cells of acute inflammation and are not the main lipid-laden cells of the fatty streak. Platelets matter later, forming thrombus when a plaque ruptures. Endothelial cells are where the injury begins and they let LDL and monocytes in, but they do not become foam cells.

questions.q: Why does rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque often cause sudden myocardial infarction even when the plaque was causing little narrowing before?
options: Rupture causes immediate coronary artery spasm, which is the main cause of infarction
The fibrous cap calcifies instantly and blocks the lumen
The ruptured plaque releases cholesterol crystals that dissolve the myocardium
Exposure of the thrombogenic core triggers platelet aggregation and a thrombus that occludes the artery
questions.why: When the fibrous cap ruptures, the lipid core and collagen are exposed to blood. Platelets adhere and aggregate and the clotting cascade forms a thrombus that can suddenly block the artery. Cholesterol crystals do not dissolve heart muscle; damage comes from loss of blood supply. Vasospasm can contribute but is not the main mechanism after rupture. Calcification develops over a long time in older plaques; it does not happen instantly at rupture.

questions.q: Outline the stages in the development of an atherosclerotic plaque and explain how risk factors such as smoking and hypertension contribute.
markScheme: Endothelial dysfunction/injury is the initiating step; smoking and hypertension damage the endothelium
LDL enters the intima and is oxidised; monocytes enter and become macrophages
Macrophages take up oxidised LDL to become foam cells, forming the fatty streak
Smooth muscle cells migrate and produce collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a lipid/necrotic core
Complications: thin-capped plaque ruptures, platelets aggregate and thrombus forms (acute coronary syndrome/stroke)
questions.modelAnswer: Atherosclerosis starts with endothelial dysfunction. Smoking (through toxins and oxidative stress) and hypertension (through mechanical stress) damage the endothelium, making it more permeable and more adhesive. LDL cholesterol enters the intima, where it becomes oxidised. Monocytes are attracted, cross the endothelium and become macrophages, which engulf oxidised LDL and become foam cells; collections of foam cells form the fatty streak. Over time smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and produce collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a core of lipid and dead cells. A stable plaque narrows the lumen slowly and may cause angina on exertion. If the cap is thin and inflamed it may rupture, exposing the thrombogenic core; platelets aggregate and a thrombus forms, which can occlude the artery and cause myocardial infarction or stroke.

questions.q: A 58-year-old has pre-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV₁ 1.5 L and FVC 3.0 L (FVC is below predicted). How should this pattern be described?
options: Obstructive and fully reversible, so it must be asthma
Restrictive, because the FVC is reduced
Normal, because FEV₁ is expected to be about half of FVC
Obstructive, because the FEV₁/FVC ratio is 0.5
questions.why: FEV₁/FVC = 1.5/3.0 = 0.5, below the 0.7 threshold, so the pattern is obstructive; FVC can also be low in obstruction because air is trapped. Calling it restrictive because FVC is reduced ignores the ratio, which is normal or high in restriction. A normal FEV₁/FVC ratio is usually above 0.7, so 'about half' is wrong. Reversibility cannot be judged from a single pre-bronchodilator test, so it cannot show the obstruction is fully reversible or prove asthma.

questions.q: Which pattern of lung damage is typical of emphysema caused by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
options: Centriacinar emphysema, worst in the upper lobes
Panacinar emphysema, worst in the lower lobes
Interstitial fibrosis with a restrictive pattern
Mucous gland hyperplasia without alveolar wall destruction
questions.why: Lack of alpha-1 antitrypsin leaves neutrophil elastase unchecked throughout the acinus, giving panacinar emphysema, mainly in the lower lobes. Centriacinar, upper-lobe emphysema is the pattern usually caused by smoking. Interstitial fibrosis is a restrictive disease, not emphysema. Mucous gland hyperplasia without alveolar destruction describes chronic bronchitis.

questions.q: Compare asthma and COPD in terms of cause, typical patient, mechanism of airflow obstruction and reversibility.
markScheme: Asthma: often atopic, frequently starts in childhood/young adulthood; COPD: usually older adult with significant smoking history (or other exposures)
Asthma: chronic (often eosinophilic/Th2) airway inflammation with hyper-responsiveness and bronchoconstriction
COPD: chronic bronchitis (mucus hypersecretion) and emphysema (alveolar wall destruction, loss of elastic recoil, airway collapse)
Asthma: obstruction variable and largely reversible; symptoms vary, e.g. worse at night
COPD: persistent, progressive obstruction not fully reversible; FEV₁/FVC < 0.7 post-bronchodilator
questions.modelAnswer: Asthma often begins in childhood or young adulthood and is linked to atopy and family history, with triggers such as allergens, viral infections, exercise and cold air. COPD usually affects older adults with a significant smoking history, though occupational dusts and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency also cause it. In asthma, chronic airway inflammation (often type 2, with eosinophils, mast cells and IgE) makes the airways hyper-responsive, so smooth muscle constricts, the wall swells and mucus is produced. In COPD, chronic bronchitis narrows the airways with mucus and inflammation, and emphysema destroys alveolar walls; the loss of elastic recoil lets small airways collapse during expiration and traps air. Asthma's obstruction is variable and largely reversible, so symptoms and peak flow fluctuate. COPD's obstruction is persistent and progressive and is not fully reversible, defined in NICE guidance by a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7.

questions.q: An ECG recorded at the standard 25 mm/s shows a regular rhythm with four large squares between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
questions.why: Each large square is 0.2 s, so the R–R interval is 0.8 s and the rate is 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min (300 ÷ 4). 375 comes from using the small-square rule (1,500 ÷ squares) with large squares. 15 comes from the opposite error: dividing 300 by the number of small squares (20). 150 would be the result if the paper speed were 50 mm/s, so each large square were 0.1 s.

questions.q: A patient with COPD who is known to be at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure is acutely unwell. Under British Thoracic Society guidance, what oxygen saturation should be targeted?
options: Below 85%, to avoid suppressing the hypoxic drive
questions.why: BTS guidance sets 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, because too much oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention. 94–98% is the target for most other acutely ill patients, so it misapplies the general target. Aiming for 98–100% reflects the mistaken belief that more oxygen is always safer. Deliberately keeping saturations below 85% overstates the 'hypoxic drive' concern and would leave the patient dangerously hypoxaemic.

questions.q: Describe how to measure blood pressure manually with a sphygmomanometer and stethoscope, and give three sources of error.
markScheme: Patient seated, rested, arm supported at heart level; correct cuff size over the brachial artery
Inflate cuff above systolic (e.g. estimate by palpating radial pulse disappearance), then deflate slowly
Systolic = first Korotkoff sound (phase I); diastolic = disappearance of sounds (phase V)
Errors: wrong cuff size (small cuff overestimates), arm not at heart level, talking/recent exercise/caffeine/smoking, white-coat effect, deflating too fast
Repeat the measurement and record arm and position
questions.modelAnswer: The patient should sit and rest for a few minutes, with the arm bared and supported at heart level. Choose a cuff whose bladder fits the arm, and place it on the upper arm over the brachial artery. Estimate systolic pressure by inflating the cuff until the radial pulse disappears, then deflate. Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery, inflate to about 20–30 mmHg above that estimate, and deflate slowly. The first Korotkoff sound (phase I) is the systolic pressure and the point where the sounds disappear (phase V) is the diastolic. Record the reading, the arm used and the position, and repeat if it is raised. Sources of error include a cuff that is too small (overestimates) or too large (underestimates), the arm hanging below heart level, the patient talking or having recently exercised, smoked or drunk caffeine, deflating too quickly, and the white-coat effect.

questions.q: Why do ACE inhibitors commonly cause a dry cough?
options: Bradykinin accumulates because ACE normally breaks it down
Aldosterone levels rise and cause airway oedema
Angiotensin II builds up in the lungs
They block β2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle
questions.why: ACE also degrades bradykinin, so inhibiting it lets bradykinin accumulate and irritate the airways, causing cough. Angiotensin II falls rather than builds up, because its production is blocked. β2 blockade is a property of non-selective beta-blockers, which can cause bronchospasm, not of ACE inhibitors. Aldosterone falls, not rises, with ACE inhibition.

questions.q: How does salbutamol relieve bronchoconstriction?
options: It blocks muscarinic M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle
It suppresses inflammatory gene transcription in airway cells
It stimulates β2 receptors, raising cAMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
questions.why: Salbutamol is a short-acting β2 agonist: β2 stimulation raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Blocking M3 receptors is how muscarinic antagonists such as ipratropium and tiotropium work. Suppressing inflammatory gene transcription describes inhaled corticosteroids. Blocking leukotriene receptors describes montelukast.

questions.q: Explain how aspirin and statins each reduce the risk of further events in a patient who has had a myocardial infarction.
markScheme: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1)
Reduces thromboxane A₂, so less platelet aggregation and thrombus formation on plaques, for the platelet's lifetime
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis; liver up-regulates LDL receptors so plasma LDL falls
Lower LDL slows plaque growth and stabilises plaques, so fewer ruptures
questions.modelAnswer: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-1 in platelets. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so thromboxane A₂ production is reduced for the rest of the platelet's life. Less thromboxane means less platelet activation and aggregation, so a thrombus is less likely to form on a damaged plaque. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Liver cells respond by making more LDL receptors, which remove LDL from the blood. Lower LDL slows plaque growth, and statins are thought to help stabilise plaques, so fewer rupture and cause further heart attacks or strokes.

questions.q: A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 80%. It is used in a population where 10% have the disease. What is its positive predictive value?
questions.why: In 1,000 people, 100 have the disease (90 true positives) and 900 do not (180 false positives), so PPV = 90/270 ≈ 33%. 90% is the sensitivity, a common confusion with PPV. 80% is the specificity. About 98.6% is the negative predictive value (720 true negatives out of 730 negative results).

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the parameters scored in NEWS2?
options: Level of consciousness or new confusion
Whether the patient is receiving supplemental oxygen
questions.why: Capillary refill time is part of a clinical ABCDE assessment but is not scored in NEWS2. Respiration rate is scored, and is often the earliest sign of deterioration. questions.q: Define sensitivity and specificity, and explain why a negative result on a highly sensitive test is useful for ruling out a disease.
markScheme: Sensitivity: proportion of people with the disease who test positive (TP ÷ (TP + FN))
Specificity: proportion of people without the disease who test negative (TN ÷ (TN + FP))
A highly sensitive test produces few false negatives
So a negative result makes the disease unlikely ('SnNOut'), especially when pre-test probability is not high
questions.modelAnswer: Sensitivity is the proportion of people who have the disease who test positive: true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative: true negatives divided by true negatives plus false positives. A highly sensitive test rarely misses the disease, so it gives few false negatives. If such a test is negative, the disease is therefore unlikely, which is summarised by the phrase 'SnNOut' (sensitive test, negative result, rules out). How confident you can be still depends on the pre-test probability: in a patient with a very high clinical suspicion a negative result may not be enough.

questions.q: A healthy 20-year-old student starts a period of moderate running. Explain how the cardiovascular and respiratory systems respond so that delivery of oxygen to working muscle increases and carbon dioxide is removed. Refer to relevant equations and control mechanisms.
markScheme: Cardiac output rises (CO = HR × SV): sympathetic β1 stimulation and reduced vagal tone raise heart rate and contractility
Stroke volume rises: increased venous return (muscle pump, respiratory pump, venoconstriction) increases preload (Frank–Starling) plus increased contractility

Local metabolic vasodilation in muscle (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine, low O₂) lowers TPR; sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from gut/skin; systolic BP rises, diastolic changes little (MAP ≈ CO × TPR)

Ventilation rises via increased tidal volume and rate; mechanisms include feed-forward central command and muscle afferents with chemoreceptor fine-tuning (arterial PCO₂ normally kept near normal in moderate exercise)
Rightward shift of O₂–Hb curve in muscle (raised PCO₂, H⁺, temperature) increases unloading; increased capillary recruitment shortens diffusion distance (Fick)
CO₂ carried as bicarbonate/carbamino; Haldane effect; increased pulmonary blood flow and ventilation remove CO₂
Pulmonary capillary recruitment improves V/Q matching and diffusion capacity
Clear structure and correct use of equations and values labelled approximate
questions.modelAnswer:
Working muscle needs much more oxygen, and both systems respond together.

Cardiac output. CO = HR × SV. At the start of exercise, signals from the motor cortex (central command) and from muscle receptors reduce vagal tone and increase sympathetic outflow. Noradrenaline acting on β1 receptors steepens the pacemaker slope of the SA node and raises heart rate, and it increases contractility. Stroke volume also rises because venous return increases: contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins (the muscle pump), deeper breathing lowers intrathoracic pressure (the respiratory pump), and sympathetic venoconstriction mobilises blood from the veins. Greater end-diastolic filling increases the force of contraction by the Frank–Starling mechanism. Cardiac output can rise several-fold, roughly four to five times resting in a fit young adult (approximate).

Distribution of flow and blood pressure. In muscle, local metabolites (CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine and low O₂) dilate arterioles, overriding sympathetic constriction, so muscle blood flow rises greatly and total peripheral resistance falls. Sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces flow to the gut and kidneys, and skin flow later rises for heat loss. Because MAP ≈ CO × TPR, the large rise in CO and fall in TPR mean systolic pressure rises while diastolic pressure changes little.

Ventilation. Minute ventilation rises through deeper and faster breaths. The quick rise at the start is driven by central command and muscle afferents; chemoreceptors (central, responding to CSF H⁺, and peripheral, in the carotid and aortic bodies) fine-tune ventilation so that arterial PCO₂ and PO₂ stay close to normal in moderate exercise. Pulmonary blood flow rises with cardiac output and previously underused capillaries, especially at the lung apices, are recruited, improving V/Q matching and increasing the surface area available for diffusion (Fick's law).

Oxygen unloading. In muscle, raised PCO₂, raised H⁺ and higher temperature shift the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right (the Bohr effect), so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given PO₂. More capillaries open, shortening the diffusion distance. Oxygen extraction therefore increases as well as delivery.

Carbon dioxide removal. Extra CO₂ enters red cells, where carbonic anhydrase converts it to bicarbonate, which leaves in exchange for chloride; some binds haemoglobin as carbamino compounds. Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂ (the Haldane effect). In the lungs, increased ventilation keeps alveolar PCO₂ low, so CO₂ diffuses out and is exhaled.

Together these changes match oxygen delivery and CO₂ removal to the rise in metabolic rate.

questions.q:
A 64-year-old man who has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years has increasing breathlessness on exertion and a morning cough with sputum. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV₁ 1.8 L (60% of predicted), FVC 3.3 L and FEV₁/FVC 0.55.
(a) Calculate his smoking history in pack-years. (2 marks)
(b) Interpret the spirometry and state the most likely diagnosis. (4 marks)
(c) Explain the pathophysiology that causes airflow limitation in this condition. (6 marks)
(d) Explain how an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist and a long-acting β2 agonist each improve airflow. (4 marks)
(e) Explain why smoking cessation is the most important intervention. (4 marks)
markScheme: (a) 20/20 × 40 = 40 pack-years
(b) FEV₁/FVC 0.55 < 0.7 post-bronchodilator = obstructive pattern not fully reversible; with smoking history and symptoms, most likely COPD
(c) Chronic bronchitis: mucous gland hyperplasia, goblet cells, inflammation and mucus narrow airways

(c) Emphysema (centriacinar in smokers): protease–antiprotease imbalance destroys alveolar walls; loss of elastic recoil and of radial traction lets small airways collapse on expiration; air trapping and hyperinflation
(d) LAMA blocks M3 receptors, preventing vagally mediated (acetylcholine) bronchoconstriction; LABA stimulates β2, raising cAMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle
(e) Smoking cessation is the only intervention shown to slow the accelerated decline in FEV₁ in smokers (Fletcher and Peto); also cuts cardiovascular and lung cancer risk
Correct, clearly set out working; no drug doses
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked = (20 ÷ 20) × 40 = 40 pack-years.

(b) The post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio is 0.55, below the 0.7 threshold, so there is airflow obstruction that persists after a bronchodilator and is therefore not fully reversible. FEV₁ is reduced to 60% of predicted. With a 40 pack-year history, exertional breathlessness and a chronic productive cough, the most likely diagnosis is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). By the GOLD spirometric grading, an FEV₁ of 50–79% of predicted is moderate (GOLD 2).

(c) COPD combines chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Cigarette smoke causes chronic inflammation of the airways with neutrophils, macrophages and CD8 T cells. In the larger airways, mucous glands enlarge and goblet cells increase, producing excess mucus that narrows the lumen and causes the productive cough; the airway walls thicken and fibrose. In the lung tissue, proteases such as neutrophil elastase, together with oxidants, overwhelm the antiproteases and destroy alveolar walls. In smokers this is usually centriacinar emphysema, worst in the upper lobes. Destroying alveolar walls removes elastic recoil, which normally drives expiration, and removes the radial traction that holds small airways open. During forced expiration the small airways therefore collapse early, trapping air behind them. This lowers FEV₁ much more than FVC, causes hyperinflation and increases the work of breathing. Loss of alveolar surface area also reduces gas exchange.

(d) A long-acting muscarinic antagonist (such as tiotropium) blocks M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle. Vagal release of acetylcholine is an important cause of airway tone in COPD, so blocking it relaxes the airways and widens them. A long-acting β2 agonist (such as salmeterol or formoterol) stimulates β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle; this raises cAMP and causes relaxation and bronchodilation. Both reduce air trapping and breathlessness, but neither reverses the structural damage.

(e) Smoking is the main cause of his disease. In susceptible smokers FEV₁ falls faster than the normal age-related decline. Stopping smoking is the intervention shown to slow this decline, a finding associated with Fletcher and Peto's work in the 1970s; lung function does not return to normal, but its rate of fall moves back towards that of a non-smoker. Stopping also reduces cough and sputum, the risk of exacerbations, and his high risk of cardiovascular disease and lung cancer. No inhaler slows the decline in the way stopping smoking does, so support to stop (behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy) should be offered at every opportunity.
